title: Vou ficar mais um mês — plans and the future
title_target: O que é que vais fazer?
goal: Talk about what's going to happen, what has to be done and what's needed — using the structures people in Portugal actually say, not the ones in grammar-book tables.
bekal: using the ending *-íssimo* to intensify adjectives

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Planos para o Natal
dialogs.intro: Early December. Lisbon is already strung with lights, and Ana asks about Budi's plans.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: O que é que vais fazer no Natal?
lines.id: What are you doing for Christmas?
lines.literal: what is it that you-go to-do at-the Christmas?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ainda não sei. Vou ficar em Lisboa, acho.
lines.id: I don't know yet. I'll stay in Lisbon, I think.
lines.literal: still not I-know. I-go to-stay in Lisbon, I-think.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não posso. O bilhete é caríssimo em dezembro.
lines.id: I can't. The ticket is really expensive in December.
lines.literal: not I-can. the ticket is most-expensive in December.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Então tens de vir a minha casa. A minha mãe faz sempre comida a mais.
lines.id: Then you have to come to my place. My mom always cooks too much food.
lines.literal: then you-have of to-come to my house. the my mother makes always food in excess.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Really? I don't want to be a bother.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Não incomodas nada! Vamos ser dez à mesa.
lines.id: You're no bother at all! There'll be ten of us at the table.
lines.literal: not you-bother nothing! we-go to-be ten at-the table.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vou levar qualquer coisa, então. O que é que posso trazer?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Traz só a tua fome! E talvez uma sobremesa da Indonésia.
lines.id: Just bring your appetite! And maybe an Indonesian dessert.
lines.literal: bring only the your hunger! and maybe a dessert of-the Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vou tentar. Preciso de encontrar os ingredientes.

lines.literal: I-go to-try. I-need of to-find the ingredients.

lines.text: Vais encontrar tudo no mercado. Combinado?

lines.text: Combinado! Vai ser o meu primeiro Natal em Portugal.

notes: **Vou fazer, not farei.** Portuguese has its own future tense (*farei*, *irei*, *comerei*), but in everyday conversation it's almost never used — it sounds like the TV news or an official letter. What people actually say is *ir* + infinitive, just like English "going to".

**Caríssimo** — the ending *-íssimo* means "very", and it packs far more punch than *muito*. *Caro* (expensive) → *caríssimo* (really expensive). *Bom* → *ótimo*. People in Portugal use it constantly, and using it makes your speech sound lively.
**Comida a mais** means "too much food". The structures *a mais* and *a menos* mark excess or shortage: *trouxeste dinheiro a mais* (you brought too much money).
**Não incomodas nada** — another double negative, where *nada* strengthens it to "not at all". Same structure as *não gosto nada* in unit 11.

**Qualquer coisa** means "anything" or "something". Its plural is irregular: *quaisquer coisas*. In conversation, *qualquer coisa* is also used to mean "if you need anything": *Qualquer coisa, telefona-me.*

**Traz!** is the *tu* command form of *trazer*. Informal commands are made from the *ele* form: *ele traz* → *traz!*, *ele come* → *come!*, *ele fala* → *fala!*. An easy rule with almost no exceptions.

grammars.title: Ir + infinitive
body: The structure is just like the "-ing" form in unit 13, only without *a*: the right form of *ir*, then the verb in the infinitive.

head: Pronoun
Structure
Meaning
rows: he / she / it is going to be

after: To negate, put *não* before *ir*: *não vou sair hoje*. To ask, just raise your voice or add *é que*: *O que é que vais fazer?*
**Object pronouns attach to the infinitive:** *vou ver-te amanhã*. If there's a puller, the pronoun jumps to the front of the whole structure: *não te vou ver amanhã*.

This structure is used even for things far ahead: *para o ano vou estudar em Coimbra* (next year I'm going to study in Coimbra). The form *estudarei* is correct, but nobody says it at the dinner table.

grammars.title: Must, need, should
body: Four structures of different strengths. Picking the right one changes the tone of your sentence.
after: **Precisar must take de** whether followed by a noun or a verb: *preciso **de** ajuda*, *preciso **de** ir*. Like *gostar de*, this is the mistake that sticks around longest.
*É preciso* doesn't name anyone, so it sounds gentler than a command: *É preciso chegar cedo* = "we need to get there early" — without pointing at anyone.

grammars.title: Intensifying adjectives with -íssimo
body: Drop the adjective's final vowel, then add *-íssimo*. It agrees in gender and number like any adjective.
after: Watch for small spelling changes in some words: *c* becomes *qu* (*rico* → *riquíssimo*), *g* becomes *gu* (*antigo* → *antiquíssimo*).
The last two aren't built from their base words at all, and both are very common. *Está ótimo!* and *Foi péssimo!* are everyday reactions you need to have.

blocks.text: **Daqui a** and **dentro de** both mean "in" for time ahead, and they're interchangeable: *daqui a uma semana* = *dentro de uma semana* = in a week. Compare *há uma semana* (a week **ago**) from unit 14 — the same span of time, pointing in opposite directions.

blocks.title: The future tense not taught here
items: Portuguese has a separate future tense formed from the infinitive + endings: *falarei*, *falarás*, *falará*, *falaremos*, *falarão*.
This form is hardly ever spoken in conversation. You'll meet it in the news, on notices and in formal writing — so recognize it when you see it, but don't use it.
There's one place where it's still alive in speech: wondering. *Será que ele vem?* = "I wonder if he's coming?" This sentence is very common, and it isn't about the future at all.
